paras: The reported lynching of two cattlemen in the Cherokee Strip was the reported killing of two men said to belong to cattleman George H. Delaney's band of cowboys at the hands of settlers near the line of No Man's Land, Indian Territory, in March 1888. Papers presented it as retribution for the killing of three squatters on Delaney's range a few days earlier. The lynching was carried only as a report from Wichita and Woodward, and the men were never named.

Delaney, described as a cattle king of the Cherokee Strip, grazed his herds where several squatters had built a cabin or huts, intending to claim land when the territory opened to settlement. According to a Wichita dispatch of March 8, the men were burned out of their log cabin on Rabbit Ear Creek on Sunday night, March 4, and shot down by a mob of cowboys, and people in the vicinity charged Delaney's men with the crime. Deputy U.S. Marshal Wood, who came to Wichita looking for Delaney, gave a different account: on Saturday Delaney and about a dozen cowboys ordered the settlers off, and in the shooting that followed the three men, Mrs. Antwerp and one cowboy were killed and the huts burned with the bodies.

The victims' names varied from paper to paper, appearing as Julius or Albert Quinn, Pedro, William or John Antwerp, and Joseph, John or Thomas George, or George Burns. Delaney was variously said to have fled to New Mexico or Arizona, to have gone north with a Mexican, or to be hiding in Wichita.

The first word of a reprisal came in the Wichita dispatch of March 9, which said that "the better class of settlers have already lynched two of the gang." A week later a Kansas City Times special from Woodward, I.T., said it was "reported here that two cattlemen have been lynched in the Cherokee strip near the line of No Man's Land." The same dispatch said the farmers of No Man's Land, "greatly excited" over the "butchery" of three settlers, had organized for protection. Neither report gave a date, a place more exact than the line of No Man's Land, or the names of the dead.

The Nicodemus Cyclone wrote that the farmers were arming, had reportedly "strung up two cowboys," and proposed to hang the "tyrants of the range" whenever they could. It added that United States soldiers were scouring the country to keep out intruders and might keep the two sides apart. No confirmation of the lynching, no inquest and no arrest of Delaney appear in the coverage.

The story reached readers mostly in brief wire items far from the territory, from Nebraska and Dakota to Texas, Minnesota and Maine. Headlines such as "Cattlemen Lynched" in the Fort Worth Daily Gazette and "Two Cattlemen Lynched" in the Phillipsburg Herald and Emporia Weekly News stated the lynching flatly, while the text below kept the hedge "it is reported." The Barton County Democrat said only that "a report existed" of the lynching, and the Ellsworth American shrank it to one line placing it in "Cherokee, Indian Territory."

Sympathy in the coverage lay with the settlers: the squatter killing was a "ghastly crime" in the Wichita dispatch and the lynchers "the better class of settlers." The Nicodemus Cyclone blamed "hirelings of the cattle kings" but printed the cattlemen's claim that the dead were cattle thieves and called the blame hard to locate. The Emporia Weekly News showed its doubts about the Wichita reports by heading Marshal Wood's account "Another Wichita Sensational Special."

The reports differ on who was lynched, calling the dead "two of the gang," "two cattlemen" or "two cowboys," and on whether the lynching had already happened by March 9 or was news at Woodward a week later. Accounts of the squatter killing also conflict, the wire version describing an ambush of a burning cabin and the marshal's version a shooting fight that also killed a woman and a cowboy.

reader.title: Reported lynching of two cattlemen in the Cherokee Strip
bases: Two independent dispatches reported that settlers or farmers had lynched two of cattleman George Delaney's men after the killing of three squatters (A4, A11, A18).

Reports from Wichita and from Woodward, I.T., said 'settlers', 'citizens' or organized farmers lynched two of Delaney's men in retribution for the killing of three squatters (A4, A7, A16, A18); every report is hearsay, no victim is named and no confirmation appears, so the killing itself is unconfirmed.

A Wichita dispatch of March 9 (A4) and a Kansas City Times special from Woodward dated March 16-17 (A11, A18) independently reported the lynching of two of Delaney's men, though both relayed it as report rather than confirmed fact.

framing.detail: Brief wire items headed 'Cattlemen Lynched' and 'Two Cattlemen Lynched' relayed the Woodward report with 'it is reported here' and no comment.
The Wichita dispatch under 'Shot Down as They Ran' called the squatter killing 'a ghastly crime' and credited the lynching to 'the better class of settlers'.

The Nicodemus Cyclone called the squatter killing 'dastardly' work of 'hirelings of the cattle kings' but gave the cattlemen's counter-claim and said it was 'difficult to definitely locate the blame'.
